title: 地元産作物の活用で小児栄養失調治療の裾野拡大へ、新研究が示唆
title_zh: 新研究：用本地种的庄稼做治疗食品，能让更多营养不良的孩子吃上药
lead: 深刻な栄養失調に苦しむ子供たちに有効な治療法は既に存在するが、実際に治療を受けられるのはごく一部に過ぎない。イスラエル・ヘブライ大学が主導した国際研究チームは、現地で栽培される作物を活用して治療食を生産すれば、この格差を縮められる可能性があると指摘している。

paragraphs: ヒヨコ豆やソルゴー、トウモロコシ、大豆を原料とする高タンパク質の治療食「ChSMS」を検証したこの研究は、学術誌『Current Developments in Nutrition』に掲載された。深刻な急性栄養失調の標準治療とされる即時使用可能治療食（RUTF）は、現行の製剤では必要とする子供のおよそ3割にしか行き届いていないという。その一因は、脱脂粉乳など富裕国で生産される高価な原料への依存にあり、低所得国における費用と供給の両面で障壁を生んでいる。

紛争や気候変動、人道支援資金の削減によって食料・栄養プログラムへの圧力が強まる中、こうした障壁は喫緊の課題となりつつある。研究者らは、地元で入手可能な原料から効果的な治療食を開発すれば、国際的なサプライチェーンへの依存を弱め、最も必要とされる地域でより安価に生産できると論じている。前臨床試験では、ChSMSは市販のピーナッツ・乳由来製剤を大幅に上回る回復効果を示し、catch-up growth（追いつき成長）も確認された。

栄養面でも優位性が明らかになった。ChSMSはエネルギーに占めるタンパク質の割合が約14％で、市販品の10％を上回り、タンパク質品質スコアも87％対69％と高かった。しかし研究者にとって、この製剤の意義は栄養組成にとどまらない。ヘブライ大学のエフラット・モンソネゴ＝オルナン氏は「治療食を地元で栽培される高品質な原料から生産できれば、高価な輸入への依存を減らし、より多くの子供に治療を届けられる」と語り、栄養品質を最優先としつつも、入手しやすさと地元生産が不可欠だと強調する。

国際的な指針もこうしたアプローチを後押ししている。以前は治療食のタンパク質の少なくとも半分を乳製品由来とすることが求められていたが、新たな指針ではこの要件が撤廃され、栄養基準を満たす非乳製品の現地調達型製剤への道が開かれた。乳製品を使わないことで、高価な輸入脱脂粉乳の必要性を排除できる可能性がある。大豆やヒヨコ豆、ソルゴー、トウモロコシの活用は、サハラ以南アフリカの地元食品メーカーや農業サプライチェーン、小規模農家を支えることにもつながる。

この手法は、輸入原料への依存軽減、生産コストの削減、地域経済の強化、そして救命につながる栄養治療をより多くの子供に届けるという、複数の課題を同時に解決し得る。研究では体重だけでなく直線的成長の回復の兆しも見られ、将来的に急性栄養失調と長期的な発育阻害の双方に対応できる製剤の可能性が示唆された。ただし今回の知見は前臨床段階にあり、子供への有効性を結論づけるには臨床試験による確認が不可欠だと研究者らは慎重に付言している。
paragraphs_zh: 这项研究检验了一种以鹰嘴豆、高粱、玉米和大豆为原料的高蛋白治疗食品“ChSMS”，论文发表在《Current Developments in Nutrition》杂志上。对于严重急性营养不良，即食治疗食品（RUTF）是标准疗法，但据研究称，目前的配方只能覆盖到大约三成需要治疗的孩子。原因之一在于，配方往往依赖富裕国家生产的高价原料，比如脱脂奶粉，这在低收入国家同时造成了成本和供应两方面的障碍。
在冲突、气候变化以及全球人道援助资金削减的背景下，粮食和营养项目承受的压力越来越大，这些障碍也变得越来越紧迫。研究人员认为，用当地能获得的原料开发出有效的治疗食品，有助于减少对国际供应链的依赖，也更容易在最需要的地方以更低成本生产。在临床前试验中，ChSMS的恢复效果明显优于市售的花生加奶配方，还观察到了追赶性生长。

在营养方面，这种配方的优势也很明显。ChSMS来自蛋白质的能量约占14%，高于市售产品的10%；蛋白质质量评分也达到87%，而市售产品为69%。但对研究人员来说，这种配方的意义不止于营养成分。希伯来大学的埃弗拉特·蒙索内戈-奥尔南表示：“如果治疗食品能用当地种植的优质原料来生产，我们就能减少对昂贵进口原料的依赖，把治疗带给更多孩子。”她强调，营养质量必须放在首位，但要让有效方案真正到达最需要的人群，价格可负担和本地生产同样不可或缺。
国际指南的变化也让这类做法更容易落地。过去要求治疗食品中至少一半的蛋白质来自乳制品，而新指南取消了这一要求，为符合营养标准的、使用本地原料的非乳制品配方打开了大门。由于新配方不含乳制品，研究人员认为它有可能省去昂贵的进口脱脂奶粉。改用大豆、鹰嘴豆、高粱和玉米，还能扶持撒哈拉以南非洲的本地食品厂商、农业供应链和小农户。
这种做法因此可以一举应对多个难题：减少对进口原料的依赖、降低生产成本、增强本地经济，并有可能让救命的营养治疗惠及更多孩子。研究人员还认为，本地生产的治疗食品有望在应对不同形式的营养不良方面发挥更大作用。研究发现了体重之外身高线性生长恢复的迹象，这意味着未来的配方有可能同时针对急性营养不良和长期发育迟缓。一种能兼顾两者的产品，将为这一重大全球健康挑战提供更高效、更省钱的思路。

For millions of children suffering from severe malnutrition, an effective treatment already exists. The problem is that many of them never receive it.
A new study led by Dr. Aurélie Bechoff, a visiting researcher at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, and Hebrew University professors Efrat Monsonego-Ornan and Ram Reifen, together with an international research team, suggests that part of the solution may lie in producing therapeutic food closer to where it is needed, using crops that are already grown locally. The study,
published
in
Current Developments in Nutrition
, examined a high-protein therapeutic food made from chickpeas, sorghum, corn and soybeans, ingredients widely available in sub-Saharan Africa.
Ready-to-use therapeutic foods, known as RUTFs, are a standard treatment for children with severe acute malnutrition. Yet according to the study, current treatment reaches only around 30% of children who need it. One of the major challenges is that conventional formulations often depend on ingredients produced in wealthier countries, including relatively expensive powdered milk, creating both cost and supply barriers in lower-income countries.
Those barriers are becoming increasingly urgent as conflict, climate change and cuts to global humanitarian funding place additional pressure on food and nutrition programs. The researchers argue that developing effective therapeutic foods from locally available ingredients could help make treatment less dependent on international supply chains and more affordable to produce in the regions where it is most needed.
The formulation tested in the study, known as ChSMS, replaces milk and peanuts with a combination of chickpeas, sorghum, corn and soybeans. In the preclinical study, it supported substantially better recovery from malnutrition than the commercial peanut-and-milk formulation tested, including catch-up growth.
The researchers found that the plant-based formulation contained more protein and had a higher protein quality score than the commercial product. ChSMS provided around 14% of its energy from protein, compared with 10% in the commercial formulation, while its protein quality score reached 87%, compared with 69%.
But for the researchers, the significance of the formulation goes beyond its nutritional composition.
"Access is one of the biggest challenges in treating childhood malnutrition," said Monsonego-Ornan of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. "If therapeutic foods can be produced from high-quality ingredients that are already grown locally, we may be able to reduce dependence on costly imports and make treatment available to many more children. The nutritional quality has to remain the priority, but affordability and local production are essential if we want effective solutions to reach the populations that need them most."
International guidelines have also begun to make such approaches more feasible. Earlier requirements called for at least half of the protein in therapeutic foods to come from dairy products, but newer guidelines have removed that requirement, opening the door to locally sourced, nondairy formulations that meet nutritional standards.
That shift could have broader economic consequences as well. Because the new formulation is dairy-free, the researchers say it could eliminate the need for expensive imported powdered milk in its production. Using crops such as soybeans, chickpeas, sorghum and corn could instead support local food manufacturers, agricultural supply chains and smallholder farmers in sub-Saharan Africa.
The approach could therefore address several challenges at once: lowering dependence on imported ingredients, reducing production costs, strengthening local economies and potentially making lifesaving nutritional treatment available to more children.
The researchers also see potential for locally produced therapeutic foods to play a broader role in addressing different forms of malnutrition. The study found signs of recovery in linear growth as well as weight, raising the possibility that future formulations could address both acute malnutrition and longer-term stunting. A product capable of targeting both conditions could provide a more efficient and cost-effective approach to a major global health challenge.
The findings are preclinical and will need to be confirmed in clinical studies before conclusions can be drawn about the formulation's effectiveness in children. However, the researchers say the results provide an important foundation for developing therapeutic foods that combine strong nutritional quality with affordability, local availability and long-term sustainability.
The study involved researchers from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, the University of Greenwich, the University of Kent, Benue State University, the University of Nottingham and partner organizations in Kenya and Ireland.
